parsed.explanation: Trans identity is not criminalised, legal gender recognition exists and functions, courts have issued recent trans- and same-sex-favourable rulings, and social acceptance has risen sharply (70% support equal rights in 2024). But the visitor-facing record carries a documented universal exposure: since martial law, holders of male gender markers are stopped at the border, with an NGO specifically helping trans people reissue documents to cross legally — a state-operated checkpoint friction reaching every trans visitor with a male marker. Gatekeeping and diagnosis barriers are severe but largely resident-facing. Hate-crime aggravation excludes gender identity; police indifference to anti-LGBT violence is documented but dated (2012–2013). No trans-specific violence campaign, imprisonment, or lethal pathway is documented; the worst operative features are border/document friction and thin recourse, placing this at the top of Reduced Risk.

entry_documents.exposure: Border guard stops of male-marker holders since martial law; document/presentation mismatch can trigger questioning; trans people need NGO-assisted document reissuing to cross legally.
entry_documents.protection: Legal gender recognition without surgery since 2016; court-ordered passport changes; foreign passport governs entry.
entry_documents.interaction: Exit/entry screening interacts with martial-law mobilisation rules; male-marker holders face the checkpoint regardless of presentation.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: No trans-specific detention documented; general custody placement rules unstated; police non-response to anti-LGBT violence documented only in 2012–2013.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Courts function and have ruled favourably on trans documents and same-sex family recognition recently (2025–2026).
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border stop could escalate to questioning, but no documented pattern of trans-detainee mistreatment exists in the record.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No facility-access restriction, bathroom rule, or ward-placement exposure documented for visitors.

care_services.exposure: Diagnosis increasingly hard to obtain (stereotypes, corruption, wartime barriers, 2026 report); humiliating military medical commission gatekeeping; no visitor-specific care denial documented.
care_services.protection: NGO and cross-border support networks assist trans women with assessments.
care_services.interaction: Care barriers are largely resident-facing; a visitor needing continuity care faces documented system friction but no ban.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Pervasive homophobia climate (2013); ex-gay movement framing trans identities as curable; taboo topics; church-linked disapproval; no state demonisation campaign documented recently.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Employment and media discrimination bans in force since 2015/2022; top official answered 'Yes!' on partnerships (2024).
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hate-crime aggravation excludes gender identity; roadmap scheduled fixes but enactment unconfirmed.

minors_guardians.exposure: Draft Civil Code would annul marriages on legal sex reassignment; surgery restricted to over-25s — resident-facing, not visitor-facing; no visitor-specific child exposure documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling parent's family status is contested domestically but no entry or custody rule touches visitors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Documented attacks in 2011–2012 with police non-response; no trans-specific violence statistics with denominators; no recent violent incident documented after 2012.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Massive police protection enabled pride with 1,500 marchers (2016); acceptance polling rose to 70.4% (2024).
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Dated incidents are weak evidence about present rates; current record shows organised public events proceeding safely.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No gender-identity hate-crime aggravation; anti-discrimination administrative liability scheduled but unconfirmed in force; border-stop remedy not documented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Working courts granting document relief and family recognition; active NGO infrastructure for document help and evacuation support.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Rule-of-law roadmap may improve recourse but is unconfirmed; open questions on mobilisation exemptions and draft Civil Code.

anchor_checks.comparison: The documented border stops of male-marker holders parallel Kestrel Isles' secondary screening — universal document friction with slow remedies — but martial-law stops are more state-directed and consequence-bearing, so this jurisdiction sits somewhat below that anchor's lightest reading, around its level or slightly under.

Like Meridia, entry rests on foreign documents, courts function, and detentions end in release; but this jurisdiction lacks confirmed gender-identity hate-crime aggravation and documents a martial-law border exposure Meridia lacks, keeping it below 0.75-C.

Branthol's registry-and-eviction system is a universal state-run enforcement apparatus with no remedy. Here the border stops are real but narrower (male markers), society is measurably accepting, courts grant relief, and NGOs operate — materially above that anchor.

Vellmaris shows brief detention with working complaints boards under protective national law. This jurisdiction's protections are thinner (no GI hate-crime statute) and its border exposure heavier, but its violence record is dated and its courts recent and favourable — slightly below 0.65-A.

parsed.synthesis: The combined regime pairs a non-criminalising legal order with functioning, recently trans-favourable courts, rising social acceptance, and a martial-law overlay that creates the sharpest visitor exposure: male-marker holders are stopped at borders and trans people need document assistance to cross legally. Diagnosis barriers and humiliating medical gatekeeping are severe but concentrate on residents; the draft Civil Code annulment clause is prospective and resident-facing. The dated violence record (2011–2013) with police indifference cannot be read as either current danger or current safety, but the present record shows protected mass pride events, active NGOs, and no documented trans-specific detention or killing. Severity if outed is low-to-moderate (friction, discrimination, no custodial pathway); the border exposure is universal for male-marker travellers but not custodial. Net: upper Reduced Risk, not Elevated, because the heaviest documented feature is tier-2/3 border and recourse friction, not organised targeting.
